A.biggest_strength: Rock-solid, bug-free interaction model with intuitive cell clicking, step/back navigation, and a clear candidates funnel bar.
A.biggest_weakness: Wrapping the 32-element array into 4 rows of 8 cells on mobile breaks the linear left-to-right interval intuition, and the page lacks deeper visual representations (like a decision tree) of why log2(n) holds.
A.interaction_feedback: Stepping forward and backward worked cleanly, the Python code highlighting stayed in exact sync, clicking any array cell updated the target instantly, and the log-scale size slider up to 10^9 updated calculations and halving bars smoothly. However, the automated Play mode runs at a fixed speed, and on narrow screens the 32 cells wrap across four rows, which disrupts the visual metaphor of shrinking a contiguous interval.

B.biggest_strength: Brilliant conceptual visual models—especially morphing the 16-element array into an explicit binary decision tree and providing an interactive log-scale staircase plot against linear scan.
B.biggest_weakness: A UI state bug in Scene 4 (Tree): updating the target while in the tree scene leaves treeN at 0, preventing probe path nodes from lighting up and generating a malformed readout string ('probes , found at...').
factual_errors: In Scene 4 (Tree view), when a user clicks a cell or enters a new target while already on that scene, the script pauses animations and resets treeN to 0, causing the readout text to render 'probes , found at...' with missing probe numbers, and leaves the tree nodes unhighlighted.
B.interaction_feedback: The 6-scene structured narrative is exceptionally clear, with elegant interval brackets, red strike-throughs for eliminated candidates, and dynamic MathML equations. Stepping through the algorithm using both on-screen buttons and keyboard shortcuts (arrows, comma/period) felt great. The Decision Tree view and the Log-Scale plot up to 1,000,000,000 elements provide unmatched explanatory depth. The 'new numbers' randomizer adds good exploratory value, and the notes table covers real-world language libraries and classic pitfalls like integer overflow. However, updating the target while in the Tree scene fails to highlight the path due to an animation pause issue.

structured_output.reasons: Page B is the clear winner because its visual explanations directly show the underlying mathematical mechanism rather than merely describing it. By morphing the sorted array into an explicit binary decision tree in Scene 4, Page B shows exactly why binary search requires at most floor(log2 n) + 1 steps—each comparison corresponds to traversing one level of the tree. Scene 5 further reinforces this with an interactive logarithmic plot up to 1 billion elements, and the accompanying notes provide high-value programming insights (addressing integer overflow and library variants). While Page A is a reliable and clean explainer, it remains a standard array walkthrough without the visual breakthroughs and depth that make Page B an extraordinary blog post figure.
